text: Panel of 212 manufacturing teams over four years. Higher share of team members who left and were replaced during the year was associated with lower supervisor-rated team performance against annual targets (standardized b = -0.18, p < .01). The authors attribute the pattern to the loss of tacit, team-specific knowledge.

Field study of 96 software teams with quarterly skills audits. Higher share of team members who left and were replaced during the year was associated with higher loss of team-specific procedural knowledge, from quarterly skills audits (standardized b = +0.28, p < .01).

Survey of 340 service teams in two retail chains. The association between share of team members who left and were replaced during the year and supervisor-rated team performance against annual targets was more positive when degree to which the team's work procedures are documented in written routines was high (interaction b = +0.31, p < .05). Documented routines are argued to buffer teams against the disruption of member exit.

Cross-sectional study of 1,105 teams in a logistics firm. Higher hours of formal training purchased for the team was associated with higher supervisor-rated team performance against annual targets (standardized b = +0.29, p < .01). The authors recommend expanding formal training budgets.

Two-wave survey of 180 hospital units. Higher average weekly workload per member relative to the firm norm was associated with lower supervisor-rated team performance against annual targets (standardized b = -0.27, p < .01).

Meta-analytic summary of 41 team studies. Units with higher number of team members showed no significant difference in supervisor-rated team performance against annual targets (standardized b = +0.02, n.s.).

Archival study of 2,300 hires in a professional services firm. Higher quality of replacement hires, from structured assessment scores at entry was associated with higher supervisor-rated team performance against annual targets (standardized b = +0.28, p < .01).
